title: Hand-mount the last section of a kids' bike tire: push the bead into the rim's center channel first, no tire lever
instruction: Finish putting this tire on the rim.
context: Bike mechanics fit tires every day (O*NET 49-3091.00, 49-3093.00), and the last stretch of a tight tire is the hard part. The middle of a rim is a deeper groove, the center channel (drop center). Pushing the tire's bead (its stiff inner edge) that is already on down into that channel shortens its path round the rim and frees a little extra length, so the last section rolls over the rim's edge by hand. The bead next to the last section pops back up as the section is lifted, so one hand holds it down in the channel while the other rolls the section over. Park Tool says to fit the bead by hand, using a tire lever only as a last resort because it can pinch the inner tube against the rim and puncture it, and to leave the valve pointing straight at the hub. Nothing on a tool or machine is adjusted: the slack comes from the rim's own shape.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0; angles round the wheel are counterclockwise from +x seen from above. A 12-inch kids' bike wheel lies flat on a hub stand clamped to the table: a dark steel post 1.8 cm across on a 12 x 12 cm foot plate, through the hub, with the hub axis at x 28, y 0 and the rim's middle plane at z 8.5. The wheel has 16 steel spokes and an aluminum rim, ISO 203 (bead seats 20.3 cm across), 2.1 cm wide outside; its flanges (the raised edges that hold the tire in) reach radius 10.6 cm (the upper flange's top at z 9.55), and its center channel (drop center) is a groove 6 mm wide and 4 mm deep round the middle of the rim (radius 9.75 cm against 10.15 cm at the bead seats), lined with a red rim strip. A 12.5 x 2.25 inch (57-203) tire with a black tread and tan sidewalls is on it, 30.3 cm across the tread, its top at z 11.35, with its inner tube inside, a little air in it. The lower bead is fully on. The upper bead (the tire's stiff inner edge) sits on its shoulder, the rim's ledge beside the flange (radius 10.15 cm, z 9.35), all round except the last section, from 60 to 120 degrees (centered at x 28, y 10, on the robot's left): there the tire's upper sidewall is tilted 20 degrees up about the tread and its bead lip rests at z 10.8, above the flange. The valve, a Schrader stem through the rim bed at 90 degrees (x 28, y 9), sticks 3.2 cm in toward the hub with a brass rim nut and a black cap and leans 20 degrees (its cap toward +x, 1.1 cm off the line to the hub). A blue nylon tire lever, 11.5 x 2.2 x 0.8 cm and 20 g, with a spoon tip toward +x and a spoke hook at the other end, lies flat on the table centered at x 20, y 21.5, along x. Both arms start at their ready pose; nothing else is on the table.
scoring: The slack comes from pushing the mounted bead down into the rim's deeper center channel, which shortens its path round the rim and frees a little extra length for the last section: each 60-degree arc pushed the full 9 mm down moves 4 mm closer to the hub and frees 4.2 mm. That length reaches the last section only through bead lying in the channel, so it is counted from each end of the section round the wheel while each arc is at least 6 mm down. The arcs beside the last section (at 30 and 150 degrees) spring back up unless held, so one hand holds one of them down while the other rolls the section; the arcs farther round stay down. The section goes over the flange only with 10 mm of slack (lifting 60 degrees of bead 4.5 mm onto the flange top takes 4.7 mm, and its climb at each end about 2.5 mm more), so the held arc and the next two at least; without it its bead stops on the flange's edge, 6 degrees short of seated. 0 (irreversible): the tire lever's spoon tip under the bead (radius 9 to 10.6 cm, at or below the bead's height there) at any control step or on its path between two, even if pulled out after: the tube is pinched. Each time, all run, the section passes 0.5 degrees (0.4 mm at its bead) beyond the flange's edge or comes into its seat: 0 (irreversible) without the slack (forced; also if it stays past the edge without slack for 3 steps), and 0 unless one gripper's pad is pressing the section and the other's is holding an arc beside it at least 6 mm down at that arc's press spot (the lever on the spot does not count). Then at the end: 0 if the section's bead is not below the flange top (within 2.6 degrees of seated) or a gripper's tool point or pad tip is within 1 cm of the tire, rim or valve (still pressing or holding). 0.5: bead on, valve stem over 10 degrees off the line to the hub (its tip over 5.6 mm off). 1.0: bead on, valve within 10 degrees, hands off; 0.9 if an arm is not back within 3 cm of its start and still. Doing nothing, rolling the section without slack, with no arc beside it held or with one hand, forcing it, and using the lever all score 0. Real trial: the bead line inside the flange all round, a protractor card on the rim for the valve angle, the video for the lever; then inflate to 40 psi and dunk the tube to confirm no pinch.
reset_notes: By hand: lift the last section back over the flange at the valve (60 to 120 degrees), pull the bead back up out of the channel onto its shoulder all round (2 to 3 psi in the tube pushes it up), deflate to the starting pressure, set the valve to 20 degrees on the protractor card and put the lever back on its tape outline. If a lever went under the bead, inflate the tube and check it for a pinch hole in water; replace it if it leaks.
fidelity: Five 60-degree bead arcs slide 9 mm down into the channel (the two beside the last section spring back up unless held) and the last section is hinged. Slack is a scored law, not rubber physics: the arcs' drops counted through the channel from the section's ends; the section stops at the flange's edge until 10 mm is freed. The tube is not simulated: a pinch is read from the lever tip's position. Only the press spots and the valve have colliders.
